canonical_topic: Outage rates and capacity auction mechanics
definition: Capacity payments are usually scaled to how much a unit is expected to actually run, based on its typical forced outage rate, and the price for capacity is generally set through an auction.
core_idea: In a capacity auction, generators bid their full capacity (unless retiring), the grid sets a target capacity need, and payments flow only if there's a shortfall relative to that target — otherwise no one is paid.
key_points: A forced outage is defined as an equipment failure or other breakdown.
Capacity compensation is typically adjusted for the unit's expected forced outage rate.
Auctions require most generation units to bid in their full capacity unless they intend to retire the unit.
The grid operator sets a target amount of capacity it believes is needed to serve demand.
If the market meets the target, no capacity payments are made; if there is a shortfall, payments are made to incentivize new construction.
This auction design works reasonably well when consumer demand is steadily rising, but tends to under-compensate existing generation when demand is flat or declining.
A separate unresolved problem is compensating standby units that run only intermittently, sometimes as rarely as once every 5-10 years.
relationships: Builds on the general capacity market concept described in the prior item.
trading_implications: In stable- or falling-demand regions, capacity auction revenue alone may be insufficient to keep existing plants economically viable.
